title: Wendell and the Letter
premise: In 1918, on a fog-bound pearl-fishing coast, sixteen-year-old Mara Eastwick has spent her indenture making herself small inside the Meridian Trading Company's counting house, copying names she was taught not to read. When the army requisitions the town and seals the ledgers as evidence of wartime profiteering, Mara realizes the ledger holds the only record of divers lost at sea — including her father — and that its destruction would erase them forever. With the help of Wendell, a half-deaf old clerk who once falsified entries to protect the divers, and Tamsin, a soldier's widow turned smuggler, Mara races to copy and distribute the names before the armistice is signed and the company's amnesty burns every page. In the end she cannot save the building or the ledger, but she saves the letter — a single page of names read aloud in the town square — and finds that justice outside the law begins with being witnessed.
about_author: Petra Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers from coastal trading towns before turning to fiction. She writes about the people history files under 'miscellaneous,' and lives within sight of the sea.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Hands
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Establishes her invisible life copying entries in the Meridian counting house, her friendship with Wendell the clerk, and her rule never to read what she writes. When soldiers arrive to requisition the town and seal the ledgers, Mara glimpses her father's name among the recorded dead. Emotional beat: the shock of discovering invisibility was a choice made for her, not by her.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Alternating Mara and Wendell POVs. Wendell confesses he altered entries for years to shield the divers; the sealed ledger now threatens everyone it ever named. Mara resolves to copy the pages before the armistice triggers an amnesty burn, and recruits Tamsin, who moves contraband through the fog. Emotional beat: fear hardening into purpose as found family forms around a shared secret.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days of Fog
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with Wendell's interludes. The copying race: nights in the sealed workshop, near-discoveries by the requisition officer Captain Voss, and Tamsin ferrying copied pages to fishing families. When Voss catches Wendell and demands he surrender the originals, Wendell takes the blame alone. Emotional beat: rising dread and sacrifice — the cost of justice outside the law becomes personal.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Armistice day: the workshop is condemned, Wendell awaits transport, and the original ledger burns. But Mara stands in the town square with the last copied page and reads the divers' names aloud while the whole town listens, Voss powerless against a crowd that refuses to look away. Wendell is released; Mara claims her own name at last. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into witness — memory as the only justice that endures.
